newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambian opposition says talks with government off.
newsitem.headline: Zambian opposition says talks with government off.

text.p: Efforts by aid donors to bring together Zambia's government and a coalition of 12 opposition parties for talks to end a poltical impasse collapsed on Monday, an opposition party official said.

The Swedish-based International Institute of Democracy and Electoral Assistance (IDEA) was set to mediate discussions, but IDEA representative Berhe Pesfu Constantinous left Zambia at the weekend after both sides failed to agree on an agenda for talks.
Foreign donors wanted discussions between President Frederick Chiluba's government and opposition parties to begin on Tuesday to ease tension between them.
Bitterness between the sides has grown since Chiluba passed a constitutional amendment keeping all real presidential challengers out of last November's general election.

The donors cut aid to Zambia at the time to pressure Chiluba into withdrawing the new law, but he refused to budge and opposition leaders now accuse the foreign governments of using talks as a pretext to restore their aid programmes.
"The talks have collapsed only because the government has refused to compromise," general secretary for the opposition Zambia Democratic Congress, Derrick Chitala, told Reuters.
"As things stand now, an inter-party conference is out of the question," he added.
But Zambia's minister without portfolio, Michael Sata, said the talks had been put off to give the opposition time to reorganise itself.
"The talks have not collapsed. It is just that the opposition does not seem to have anything to talk about," Sata said. "When they are ready we will talk.
"Everyone, including the donors knows that the opposition is just not ready for dialogue," Sata added.
Donors have told the government the aid squeeze would be eased at a Consultative Group of donors meeting in Paris next month -- provided that the government begins dialogue with the opposition.

The government, who has instituted sweeping economic reforms and a massive programme of privatising hundreds of state-owned firms, is anxious to restore normal relations with donors. It is banking on aid to fund a third of the country's $1.1 billion budget for 1997.
The country needs about $200 million in balance of payments support and $275 million in project financing in 1997.
